NATIONAL PARK SERVICE | HISTORIC PRESERVATION CERTIFICATION APPLICATION | PART 1 -
EVALUATION OF SIGNIFICANCE
Part 1 - Evaluation of Significance

Ie Owner of record: Calder Works Owner LLC, a Virginia limited liability company,
acting by its duly authorized signatory, which certifies that it holds fee simple
title to the property described below and has authority to make this application.

2. Property: the former Calder Shoe Company works, 1200 Commerce Street,
Lynchburg, VA 24504, situated within the boundaries of the Lower Basin
Historic District as listed in the Virginia Landmarks Register and the National
Register of Historic Places.

z Request: a determination, for each structure identified in Section 5, as to
whether the structure contributes to the significance of the registered historic
district for purposes of Section 47 of the Internal Revenue Code.

NPS - DETERMINATION ISSUED
une 12, 2023
Calder Works | Partl Evaluation of Significance Page 1 of 8

Section 1 - Description and significance

L Building A is a four-story brick factory with a reinforced concrete frame, steel
sash windows and a fired-clay cornice and frieze along Commerce Street.

2. Alterations within the period of significance include the 1931 freight elevator
addition; later alterations are limited to infilled loading bays on the river
elevation.

Calder Works |. Partl Evaluation of Significance Page 2 of 8

Section 5 - Determinations by structure

of The complex consists of three structures on a single tax parcel, historically
operated as an integrated shoe manufacturing works under common ownership
until 1958, when production ceased and the property passed to a succession of
warehousing tenants.

6. Of the three structures, the two reinforced-concrete-frame masonry factory
buildings erected in 1924 and 1928 (identified in this application as Buildings A
and B) retain integrity of location, design, setting, materials, workmanship,
feeling and association sufficient to convey the significance of the district, and
are determined to contribute to that significance.

Vs The single-story concrete-block annex erected in 1968 (identified as Building C)
post-dates the close of the district's period of significance, lacks the materials
and workmanship characteristic of the contributing resources, and is
determined to be non-contributing; accordingly, Building C is not a certified
historic structure within the meaning of 36 CFR 67.2, and costs attributable to
it are outside the scope of any certification issued for the complex.

Part 2 - Description of Rehabilitation: Decision
August 14, 2023
Calder Works Owner LLC, c/o Halvorsen Urban Partners LLC. Project: Calder Shoe
Company Works, 1200 Commerce Street, Lynchburg, VA 24504. NPS Project No.
51-2023-0447.
The National Park Service has reviewed the Description of Rehabilitation and has
determined that the proposed rehabilitation will be consistent with the historic
character of the property and the district, and will meet the Secretary of the Interior's
Standards for Rehabilitation, only if the conditions set forth on page 4 of this decision
are met. This determination does not constitute certification of the completed project,
which may be denied if the conditions are not satisfied or if the work as completed
departs from the work described.
NPS - APPROVED WITH CONDITIONS
August 14, 2023

Project summary as represented by the applicant

i. Use after rehabilitation: residential rental apartments with resident amenity
space on the ground floors.

2. Phasing: the applicant represents that Building A will be completed and
occupied before work on Building B is completed.

3. Scope: rehabilitation of Buildings A and B. Building C, determined
non-contributing in Part 1, is not included in the work reviewed under this
application, and nothing in this decision should be read as a determination
regarding work on Building C.

4. Architect of record: Moss & Varner Architects, Richmond, Virginia.

Item 5
Existing feature and condition: Masonry: repoint with lime-based mortar matched to
the original in color, texture and compressive strength; replace spalled brick in kind.
Proposed work and impact on the feature: the work will be undertaken in accordance
with the Standards and the drawings and photographs referenced for this item.

Calder Works | Part2 Decision and Description Page 3 of 30

Conditions of approval

Condition 1 The fired-clay (terra cotta) cornice and frieze on the Commerce Street
elevation of Building A are character-defining features. They must be
retained and repaired in situ. Replacement of individual units may be
undertaken only where a unit is documented in the conditions survey as
deteriorated beyond repair, and then only in kind, matching the original
in material, color, profile and finish. The use of substitute materials,
including glass-fiber-reinforced concrete, fiberglass or cast stone, has
not been reviewed and is not approved.

Condition 2 The central light court of Building B is a character-defining feature and
shall remain open to the roof for its full height. No new floor plates or
infill within the light court are approved. The applicant shall submit, as
an amendment to this application, revised floor plans reflecting the
resulting reduction in the number of dwelling units.

Any proposal affecting the work described in Conditions 1 and 2 must be submitted to

the State Historic Preservation Office as an amendment for review by the National

Park Service before the work is undertaken.

Residential Market Study
     Calder Works, Lynchburg, Virginia | Prepared for Halvorsen Urban Partners LLC | March 20, 2023

Summary of findings
1.      This study evaluates demand for the adaptive reuse of the Calder Shoe Company works as market-rate
        rental housing within the Lower Basin submarket of downtown Lynchburg.
2.      For purposes of this analysis we have assumed the development program furnished by the sponsor in
        February 2023, comprising approximately 134 dwelling units distributed across all three structures on
        the site, together with ground-floor amenity space; the sponsor has advised that this program is
        preliminary and may change upon completion of historic review and final design, and our conclusions
        should be revisited if the unit count changes materially.
3.      On that basis, the market can support the subject at the proposed rents, with stabilization within
        approximately fifteen months of first delivery.




Calder Works | Market Study 2023                                                                      Page 1 of 40

Downtown housing
4.      Downtown Lynchburg has seen steady conversion of former warehouse and industrial buildings into
        rental housing over the past decade. Recent conversions in the Lower Basin have stabilized within
        twelve to fifteen months and report occupancy above ninety-four percent.
5.      The Lynchburg metropolitan area has a diversified economic base anchored by higher education,
        healthcare, advanced manufacturing and nuclear energy services. Employment has recovered to above
        pre-2020 levels, and the unemployment rate remains below the statewide average.
6.      Renter households in the primary market area are younger and more likely to be single-person
        households than the regional average. Graduate students, hospital staff and young professionals
        represent the core demand segments for loft-style units.
7.      Principal risks include delays in construction, competition from pipeline projects, and sensitivity of the
        renter base to local employment conditions. These risks are mitigated by the subject's location, historic
        character and limited competing supply in the immediate area.




Calder Works | Market Study 2023                                                                       Page 2 of 40

Pipeline
8.      Two projects totaling 210 units are in the development pipeline, of which one is under construction.
        The pipeline is modest relative to projected household growth and is not expected to materially affect
        lease-up of the subject.
9.      Five comparable properties were surveyed, ranging from 48 to 162 units. Three are adaptive reuse
        projects and two are newer garden-style communities. Rents at the adaptive reuse projects carry a
        premium of eight to twelve percent over the garden-style properties.
10.     Achievable rents for the subject were derived from the comparable survey with adjustments for unit
        size, finishes, parking and amenities. The concluded rents support the proposed unit mix and are
        consistent with recent leasing at the most comparable properties.
11.     Absorption at comparable adaptive reuse properties has ranged from seven to eleven units per month.
        A pace of nine units per month is supported for the subject, assuming marketing begins ninety days
        before the first units are delivered.

II.A Transferability
1.      Section 6418 permits an eligible taxpayer to elect to transfer all or a portion of an eligible credit, which
        is defined by cross-reference to an enumerated list in Section 6418(f)(1). The rehabilitation credit
        determined under Section 47 does not appear in that list. It follows that the federal credit generated by
        the Buildings cannot be transferred by election to an unrelated purchaser, and any description of such a
        transfer in offering or investor materials is incorrect. The credit may be shifted to a lessee only by an
        election under Section 50(d), as discussed in Part III.
2.      We recommend that every statement in presentations, summaries or correspondence describing a
        Section 6418 sale of the federal credit be withdrawn and replaced with a description of the lease
        pass-through.

7.      If a building is disposed of, or ceases to be investment credit property, within five years after it is
        placed in service, a portion of the credit is recaptured. The recapture percentage declines by twenty
        percentage points for each full year the property is held. A transfer of an interest in the lessee
        partnership can also cause recapture in a pass-through structure.

        amount equal to the qualified rehabilitation expenditures of the lessor, and the lessee, rather than the
